content.title: Response to reviewer feedback and withdrawal of submission
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their comments. We want to address the issue of GraphCodeBERT doing worse than CodeBERT in our reported results, mainly due to their relative performances on CodeSearchNet. 

There was an issue with the input being passed to CodeBERT as the code snippet candidates included the entire query in their docstring as comments which had made it easier for CodeBERT to just match these with the query while ignoring the code part, leading to inflated numbers. This issue wasn't there for GraphCodeBERT as the docstrings were already being removed. Once we made this correction for CodeBERT, we observed the rectified results to be below their GraphCodeBERT counterparts for all variants.

We also want to quickly address the missing citations in our work. We acknowledge that comparisons with these approaches are necessary and they should have been covered in the related work section of our paper. The approach "Towards Learning (Dis)-Similarity of Source Code from Program Contrasts" (DISCO) comes closest as it is very relevant to our work in terms of the AST and CFG-based rules it defines. However, many proposed rules for C++/Java do not always apply to Python; especially rules related to datatypes (e.g. replacing int with short int) as Python has dynamic data typing and can handle much longer integers as well as switching between integers and floats through implicit type conversions.

We are choosing to withdraw our submission based on the feedback received from reviewers to conduct more experiments to show the necessity of curriculum learning (beyond comparison with naive curricula and dynamic negative sampling).

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper uses two ideas to improve code search: creation of hard negatives through ASTs and changing operators and curriculum learning. The experimental results are comprehensive. The paper demonstrates gains on three models: CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, UniXCoder, on four datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
(+) Code search is an important problem and the paper uses ASTs to generate negative examples.

(+) The experiments are comprehensive.

(-) The role curriculum learning is not quantified. This needs an ablation study.

(-) Hard negatives bring down performance. This needs a discussion.

(-) Several of the transformations in Table 2 do not need AST. The claim of AST-based negatives is getting weaker.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation is clear. The ideas have limited novelty and are not thoroughly examined. The results should be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper contains some interesting ideas. Both the ideas and the experimental validation have gaps. The need for AST, the effectiveness of curriculum training are not fully explored. Data augmentation now fairly standard. The paper can also report how many negative samples are generated.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a neural model for code search that is trained on hard negative samples (generated by AST perturbation) and using curriculum learning. The experiments show promising results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

+ important problem.
+ incorporating curriculum learning for code embedding is novel.
+ Promising Results

Weakness
- Use of negative sampling for code embedding is not new. In fact, the paper completely missed the closest related work 
"Ding, Yangruibo, et al. "Towards Learning (Dis)-Similarity of Source Code from Program Contrasts." Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2022."
I will encourage the author to elaborate on how they are different and, if possible, compare them. 

- Authors only tested on code search. However, the embedding can be pretty generic. Why did such embedding not be applied to other code-related tasks (especially while authors motivated using code generation, bug finding, etc.?

- The rationale behind how to choose soft vs hard negative samples is not clear.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Although the usage of curriculum learning is novel in code-related tasks, previous works used positive and negative examples in contrastive learning settings. Without the comparison of such baseline(s), it is not clear how impactful curriculum learning is.
Thus, overall the paper lacks some novelty and needs to clarify many design choices as mentioned under weakness.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed approach shows promising results. However, they miss important baseline comparisons and might not be generalizable for other tasks.

content.summary_of_the_paper: To address the problem that current pre-trained models often retrieve the code snippets with the wrong data type and wrong method name, this paper introduces a new approach that constructs the hard negative samples through AST perturbations with a mastering-rate-based training curriculum approach to improve the performance of representation learning in the fine-tuning stage. This paper conducts the experiment with three pre-trained models and the proposed approach outperforms all the baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

Previous research has noticed that current pre-trained models often retrieve the code snippets with wrong data type or method names, this paper proposes the approach to improve the learnt representation to address this problem. The paper is generally well written and is easy to follow. The experiment results also demonstrate that the proposed approach can further improve the performance of pre-trained models in the fine-tuning stage compared to the regular contrastive learning.

Weaknesses:

First of all, the novelty of this paper is limited. The paper adopts AST perturbations to construct the hard negative samples with curriculum training for contrastive learning in the task of code search. However, such a method is not entirely new and some previous approaches have already adopted similar ideas for the construction of the samples. For example:

Li et al., CodeRetriever: Unimodal and Bimodal Contrastive Learning for Code Search, https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10866.

Shi et al., Enhancing Semantic Code Search with Multimodal Contrastive Learning and Soft Data Augmentation, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.03293.pdf

Xiao Wang et al., HELoC: hierarchical contrastive learning of source code representation. In Proceedings of the 30th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Program Comprehension (ICPC '22), 354–365. 

Secondly, the motivation of the paper is to address the problem of code retrieval with the wrong data type, method name, or signatures. However, the paper only presents the overall performance of fine-tuned models. How many (and what percentage) of the incorrect code retrieval with such problems have been fixed need to be described.

Thirdly, about the selection of batch size for the baselines GraphCodeBERT and CodeBERT, it is well known that the code search performance of GraphCodeBERT is better than the performance of CodeBERT and the batch size plays a key role in the performance improvement in contrastive learning. But this paper sets different batch sizes for CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT, which leads to worse performance of GraphCodeBERT compared to CodeBERT. What’s more, either batch size of 48 or 32 is relatively small for the current contrastive learning setting. It is better to conduct the performance experiment with a larger batch size to check if the proposed approach still works well in a larger batch size setting.

Fourthly, the performance improvement of the proposed approach is not significant. The contrastive learning with Dynamic Negative Sampling can achieve close performance as the proposed approach and even outperforms the proposed approach in the in-domain and out-of-domain experiments. What’s more, it can be found that the performance improvement on the UniXcoder is very small.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is generally well written and is easy to follow. The experiment results demonstrate that the proposed approach could be effective. The novelty is limited. The implementation of the method is not available for replication study.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper introduces a new approach to construct hard negative samples to further improve the models’ performance with contrastive learning. However, the novelty of the proposed approach is limited, more experiment results also need to be supplied. The performance improvement of the proposed approach is not very significant.

content.title: SYNC: Efficient Neural Code Search Through Structurally Guided Hard Negative Curricula
content.TL;DR: This paper proposes an AST-guided hard negative sampling method for training efficient neural code search models using curriculum learning.
content.abstract: Efficient code snippet search using natural language queries can be a great productivity tool for developers (beginners and professionals alike). Recently neural code search has been popular, where a neural method is used to embed both the query (NL) and the code snippet (PL) into a common representation space; which is further used to obtain the most relevant PL satisfying the intent in the query. Transformers-based pre-trained language models (such as CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, UniXCoder) have been especially effective to learn such representation. These models often make mistakes such as retrieving snippets with incorrect data types, and incorrect method names or signatures; even when exposed to the underlying structural information of the code (such as Abstract Syntax Tree and other static analysis outputs) during pre-training. The generalization ability beyond the training data is also limited (as the code retrieval datasets vary in the ways NL-PL pairs are collected). In this work, we propose a structure-aware hard negative sampling method and a mastering-rate based curriculum learning technique (SYNC) that enhances the pre-trained representation using both soft (random) and the (synthesized) hard negative samples. Our experiments on three state-of-the-art pre-trained language models for programming languages, over four Python code retrieval datasets, show the efficacy of the approach (under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings).
